messages.subject: advanced.ProcD.lm with 3 predictors and interactions
parts:
Hi All,

I'm analyzing data from an experiment in which individuals from different sites were run through an experimental test (each at their home site). Individuals either failed or succeeded at the challenge. I'm interested in whether body shape contributes to success in this challenge, after controlling for the effects of centroid size and site of origin.

I'm wondering how to include interactions between these three predictors, and how to test for their effects using the advanced.procD.lm framework. I think that all possible interactions might reasonably be hypothesized to have an effect on body shape as described below. 

size - allometry
site - mean population differences
success - functional effect of body shape on success
size:site - allometric trajectory differs by population
size:success - success depends on allometric component of shape
site:success - success depends on site-based differences in shape
size:site:success - success depends on site-based differences in the allometric trajectory of shape. 

Following Collyer et al 2015 (A method for analysis of phenotypic change for phenotypes described by high-dimensional data) and these helpful blog posts I tried to start with the full model and then iteratively test against a reduced model by pulling out one interaction term at a time. Then, when I only had terms that were significant I would have to consider adding ~groups and ~slope terms.

On my first iteration the 3-way interaction did not significantly improve model fit so I dropped it. How do I decide which two-way interaction to test next? If one (for example, site:success) is significant, do I try to test/drop the others or do I stop there? I think I'm ultimately interested in the LS means of the different levels of site:success. The LS means output differ depending on which other predictors are included in the model and I'm unsure how to determine which set of predictors is appropriate to include.

Thanks for your help and consideration.

Best,
Ben
